newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end up; home sales, strong dlr cited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end up; home sales, strong dlr cited.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended higher on Monday, aided by a combination of a strong dollar, central bank buying and a weak report on October U.S. home sales.
The market opened marginally lower but promptly drew in some bids, aided by a firm dollar.

The government's report that sales of existing homes slipped to an annualized rate of 3.97 million in October from a revised 4.03 million in September, adding to the accumulated evidence of a slower economy at the start of the fourth quarter, also lent the market support.

"The dip was in line with consensus, but what people did not expect was a year-over-year home price increase of only 2.8 percent," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A., an independent economic research group. "Also, the inventory of unsold homes pushed above seven months."
Stiles called the housing data "a mild positive" for the bond market.
Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at CS First Boston, said there were consistent accumulations of positions for most of the day. Retail investors "nibbled" at the market, he said.

Activity early in the session was largely Street dominated when a strong dollar, friendly economic data and later, central bank buying in the five-year area of the curve forced people to cover short positions, strategists said.

"The rally here left some people short and they have to catch up," said Alexy. He said thanks to the rally and to its extension after the well-bid Treasury quarterly refunding operation earlier this month, portfolio managers' benchmark maturity indices had lengthened relative to their average portfolio durations.
"So they have to buy securities to stay neutral," he said.
Not surprisingly though, the market was unable to hold the best of the day's gains.

"Good central bank buying in the five-year area of the yield curve seemed enough to get things going a little higher but then we ran up against some important resistance levels," said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC.
For the cash 30-year bond yield, that area of resistance was anything below 6.40 percent. The December T-bond futures contract ran into resistance at 115-25, below its nine-month high of 115-29.

A wire-service story that the Federal Reserve would eliminate bank reserve requirements briefly lifted the market "because some guys in the futures pit felt eliminating reserve requirements would leave banks flush with cash and interest rates would fall," said Dimick.
But Dimick said that hope was countered by the view that the Fed would neutralize any stimulative tendency that a change like that might spawn.
The 6-1/2 percent 30-year bond ended at 100-31/32, up 6/32 to yield 6.43 percent.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed flat at 5.03 percent. The six-month bill rate rose one basis point to 5.07 percent. The year bill rate was down one basis point to 5.14 percent.

Two-year notes rose 1/32 to end at 99-29/32, yielding 5.67 percent. Five-year notes rose 1/32 to finish at 99-25/32, yielding 5.93 percent. Ten-year notes rose 2/32 to 102-22/32, yielding 6.13 percent.
